title: Making plans with friends
goal: Ask friends if they're free, suggest a plan, fix where to meet, say you're on your way or running late, and cancel without offending anyone.
intro:
Welcome to Part 2. From here on the course is about the Urdu you need with friends, in town and at work — the way people in Karachi, Lahore and Islamabad (and Pakistanis in London or Toronto) actually talk.

We start with plans. You'll learn the friendly **'let's'** (**چلو، چلتے ہیں!**), how to boss your friends around nicely with **تم** commands and the little word **نا**, and how to say you're **about to leave** (**نکلنے والا ہوں**) or **on your way** (**راستے میں ہوں**) — even when you haven't left yet.

Young people also say بزی bizī.

کہیں چلیں؟ = shall we go somewhere?; کہیں نہیں = nowhere
The تم-command of چلنا, used to start a suggestion: چلو، چلتے ہیں = come on, let's go. Polite: چلیں.
f. فلم لگی ہے = a film is showing
m
m. ڈنر کرنا = to have dinner; at home people still say رات کا کھانا.
m
Also ساتھ: سب ساتھ چلیں گے.
After a command it coaxes: آ جاؤ نا! = oh come on, come! After a statement it asks for agreement: تم آ رہے ہو نا؟ = you are coming, right? Not the same as نہ "not".
مت جاؤ = don't go. Blunter than نہ جاؤ; never with آپ.
f. The way most young men get around; friends ride two or three to a bike.

grammar.title: Let's… and shall we…?
grammar.body:
Urdu has three everyday ways to suggest doing something together.

**1. چلو + the ہم form of the present habitual** — the most common 'let's' among friends. It literally says 'come on, we do X': چلو، کچھ **کھاتے ہیں** 'come on, let's eat something'; چلو، **چلتے ہیں** 'let's go'. The verb is always **-تے ہیں**. Without چلو it still works: سات بجے **ملتے ہیں** 'let's meet at seven'. **ایسا کرتے ہیں…** means 'tell you what, let's…'.

**2. The subjunctive (from unit 18)** for 'shall we…?': ہم کب **ملیں**؟ 'when shall we meet?', **چلیں**؟ 'shall we go?', فلم **دیکھیں**؟ 'shall we watch a film?'. **کیوں نہ** + subjunctive = 'why don't we…': کیوں نہ مال میں **ملیں**؟

**3. Going somewhere to do something:** oblique infinitive (-نے) + چلنا / جانا: فلم **دیکھنے** چلتے ہیں 'let's go and see a film', چائے **پینے** چلیں؟ 'shall we go for tea?'.

To ask what the others think, add **کیا خیال ہے؟** 'what do you think?'. 'Let me…' is **مجھے … دو**: مجھے **سوچنے دو** 'let me think'.

**Trap:** چلو + **-تے ہیں** means 'let's'; چلو + **-و** is an order to the other person: چلو، **کھاؤ** = 'come on, eat (you)!'.

examples.en: Shall we go out somewhere tonight?

examples.en: Tell you what — let's meet at seven.

examples.en: Let's go to the beach — what do you think?

grammar.title: Commands among friends: تم, تو, نا and مت
grammar.body:
You met the three imperatives in unit 11. With friends, this is how they are really used:

**تم form (-و)** — the normal way to tell a friend what to do: **آؤ**، **بتاؤ**، **سنو**، **چلو**. Use it with friends, younger siblings and cousins.
**تو form (bare stem)** — **آ**، **بتا**، **سن**، **چل**. Between very close friends or brothers it sounds warm (چل یار!); to anyone else it is rude.
**آپ form (-یے / -یں)** — for a friend's parents, elders, colleagues, strangers.

**Making it friendlier:**
- add **نا** after the verb to coax: آ جاؤ **نا**! 'oh, come on, come!', بتاؤ **نا**! 'go on, tell me!'
- use a compound with **جانا / دینا**: آ **جاؤ** 'come (over)', بتا **دو** 'just tell me' — it sounds more natural than plain آؤ / بتاؤ.
- add **ذرا** 'just': **ذرا** سنو 'listen a sec'.

**Don't:** **نہ** + verb (نہ جاؤ) or the blunter **مت** (مت جاؤ). Never use مت with آپ, and never نہیں with an imperative.

**Do it later:** the **infinitive** works as a command for later: پہنچ کر فون **کرنا** 'call when you get there', بھولنا مت 'don't forget'. With دینا it's a friendly reminder: فون کر **دینا**.

examples.en: Give me a call when you get there.
Come on, mate, let's go! (very close friends)
Just tell me what the plan is.

grammar.title: About to, on the way: نکلنے والا ہوں
grammar.body:
**About to:** oblique infinitive (-نے) + **والا / والی / والے** + ہونا. You used it for the weather in unit 13 (بارش ہونے والی ہے); it works for people too:

میں **نکلنے والا** ہوں 'I'm about to leave' (man) · **نکلنے والی** ہوں (woman) · ہم **نکلنے والے** ہیں (we)
فلم **شروع ہونے والی** ہے 'the film's about to start' (فلم is f)

Add **بس** for 'just about to': **بس** پہنچنے والا ہوں.

**Right now / any minute:** the present continuous also covers the very near future: میں **آ رہا ہوں** 'I'm coming', پانچ منٹ میں **پہنچ رہا ہوں** 'I'll be there in five minutes'.

**Already set off:** **نکل گیا ہوں** 'I've left', **راستے میں ہوں** 'I'm on the way'. Not yet: ابھی **نہیں نکلا** 'haven't left yet'.

**Running late:** either the person — **لیٹ ہو جاؤں گا** — or the dative — **مجھے دیر ہو جائے گی** (دیر is f, so ہو جائے **گی**).

examples.en: We're about to eat — come over.

culture:
Plans in Pakistan are made late and loosely, usually in a WhatsApp group, and **'five minutes'** is famously elastic. Still, if you're running late, a quick **راستے میں ہوں** keeps everyone happy — even if you're still at home.

Saying a flat 'no' sounds cold. Give a reason (**کل امتحان ہے**, **گھر پر مہمان ہیں**), say **سوری یار**, and offer another day: **کسی اور دن رکھ لیتے ہیں**. **ان شاء اللہ** can be a sincere 'hopefully' or a polite way of not committing — you'll learn to hear the difference. Many young people, especially women, also need to check with family first: **گھر والوں سے پوچھنا پڑے گا** is a perfectly normal answer.

Use **تم** with friends; the **تو** form (چل، آ، بتا) is only for very close friends and sounds rude otherwise. If you ring a friend's house and a parent picks up, switch straight to **آپ** and **جی**: **السلام علیکم انکل، علی گھر پر ہے؟**

Favourite hangouts: in Lahore, MM Alam Road, Liberty and the food streets; in Karachi, Sea View, Do Darya and Burns Road; in Islamabad, F-6 Kohsar Market and the drive up to Monal or Daman-e-Koh. Late-night chai at a **ڈھابہ** is a national institution — and in London, Bradford or Toronto the Pakistani chai spots fill up the same way.

tip.title: Friends get تم, their parents get آپ
tip.body:
- With friends: **تم** فارغ **ہو**؟ — تم کیا کر رہے **ہو**؟
- Add **یار** and you sound like a local: یار، کیا پلان ہے؟
- A friend's mum or dad picks up? Switch to **آپ** and **جی**: انکل، علی گھر پر ہے؟
- **فارغ** 'free' ↔ **مصروف** 'busy'.

tip.title: Let's: چلو … چلتے ہیں
tip.body:
- Friends say 'let's' with the **ہم** present: چلو، کھانا **کھاتے ہیں** 'let's eat'.
- 'Shall we…?' uses the subjunctive: کہاں **ملیں**؟ سنیما **چلیں**؟
- Go and do: **-نے** + چلنا: فلم **دیکھنے** چلتے ہیں.
- Trap: چلو، **کھاؤ** is 'come on, (you) eat!', not 'let's eat'.

lessons.title: Come on, don't stress!

tip.title: Friendly commands: آ جاؤ نا! مت لو
tip.body:
- Friends get the **-و** form: آؤ، بتاؤ، چلو. Very close friends: bare stem **چل، آ** (rude to others).
- Coax with **نا**: آ جاؤ **نا**! Soften with **ذرا** or a compound: بتا **دو**.
- Don't: **نہ** or blunter **مت** — never نہیں.
- For later: infinitive + دینا: فون کر **دینا** 'give me a call'.

lessons.title: I'm on my way

tip.title: About to: نکلنے والا ہوں
tip.body:
- **-نے + والا / والی / والے + ہونا** = about to: میں **نکلنے والا** ہوں, سارہ **نکلنے والی** ہے.
- **بس** = 'just': بس پہنچنے والا ہوں.
- The present continuous covers 'any minute now': پانچ منٹ میں **پہنچ رہا ہوں**.
- Already left: **نکل گیا ہوں** · **راستے میں ہوں**.

new: پانچ منٹ میں پہنچ رہا ہوں۔

sentences.native: سارہ گھر سے نکلنے والی ہے۔

lessons.title: Running late or can't make it

tip.title: Saying no nicely
tip.body:
- Say sorry and give a reason: **سوری یار**، کل امتحان ہے.
- **آج نہیں ہو سکے گا** 'it won't work out today' is softer than میں نہیں آؤں گا.
- Offer another time: **کسی اور دن** رکھ لیتے ہیں.
- Late: **میں لیٹ ہو جاؤں گا** = **مجھے دیر ہو جائے گی**.

new: یار، تھوڑا لیٹ ہو جاؤں گا۔
سوری یار، آج نہیں ہو سکے گا۔
کسی اور دن رکھ لیتے ہیں۔
